A 42-year-old man with a medical history of HIV (on dolutegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir, last CD4 count 181 nine months prior), chronic sacral osteomyelitis, multidrug-resistant bacteremia (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus epidermidis three months prior, Pseudomonas aeruginosa nine months prior), pulmonary fibrosis, and overactive bladder with a chronic indwelling Foley catheter presented with progressively worsening shortness of breath. On arrival at the emergency department, he was acutely hypoxic and rapidly deteriorated, requiring urgent intubation. He was found to be in septic shock, with a blood pressure of 72/42 mmHg and a mean arterial pressure of 52 mmHg, necessitating vasopressor support and admission to the intensive care unit (ICU) for close monitoring and management.

events.description: Death attributed to Serratia cavitary pneumonia with severe septic shock

evidence.quote: expired within 24 hours
cause of death was determined to be S. marcescens cavitary pneumonia complicated by severe septic shock

A 42-year-old man with a medical history of HIV (on dolutegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir, last CD4 count 181 nine months prior), chronic sacral osteomyelitis, multidrug-resistant bacteremia (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus epidermidis three months prior, Pseudomonas aeruginosa nine months prior), pulmonary fibrosis, and overactive bladder with a chronic indwelling Foley catheter presented with progressively worsening shortness of breath. On arrival at the emergency department, he was acutely hypoxic and rapidly deteriorated, requiring urgent intubation. He was found to be in septic shock, with a blood pressure of 72/42 mmHg and a mean arterial pressure of 52 mmHg, necessitating vasopressor support and admission to the intensive care unit (ICU) for close monitoring and management.

Empiric broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy was initiated, including vancomycin, meropenem, and anidulafungin, with an additional dose of tobramycin administered. Stress-dose corticosteroids were also started. Initial blood cultures revealed gram-negative bacilli, and the BioFire panel was positive for S. marcescens by PCR. Definitive blood cultures subsequently grew Serratia marcescens after 48 hours, at which time the patient had already expired. The isolate was resistant to ampicillin, ampicillin/sulbactam, aztreonam, cefazolin, ceftriaxone, and gentamicin (Table 1). Endotracheal aspirate cultures also grew S. marcescens with an identical resistance pattern (Table 2). In addition, urine cultures yielded S. marcescens with a similar resistance profile (Table 3).

Despite aggressive supportive care and broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy, the patient’s clinical condition deteriorated within 24 hours of presentation. Following discussions with the family and the palliative care team, his code status was changed to do-not-resuscitate (DNR), while mechanical ventilation was continued. The patient subsequently suffered a pulseless electrical activity cardiac arrest and expired within 24 hours. The cause of death was determined to be S. marcescens cavitary pneumonia complicated by severe septic shock.

summary.text: A 42-year-old man with HIV on dolutegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir (last CD4 181 nine months earlier), chronic sacral osteomyelitis, pulmonary fibrosis, overactive bladder with chronic Foley and prior MRSE/Pseudomonas bacteremia presented with progressive dyspnea. He rapidly developed acute hypoxic respiratory failure requiring urgent intubation and septic shock (BP 72/42, MAP 52) requiring vasopressors and ICU admission. Initial results showed neutrophilic leukocytosis with bandemia, AKI and severe metabolic acidosis (pH 7.05, bicarbonate 7), with lactate 1.7 mmol/L.

Imaging showed multifocal airspace disease and a right-upper-lobe cavity 10 x 7 x 12 cm with thick wall and no fluid level; CT found no abdominal/pelvic source. Empirical vancomycin, meropenem, anidulafungin, an additional tobramycin dose and stress-dose corticosteroids were given. Initial blood culture/PCR identified gram-negative bacilli/Serratia, while the definitive Serratia blood culture returned postmortem at 48 hours. Aspirate and urine also grew Serratia; all three susceptibility panels are retained separately, including susceptible meropenem and urine-resistant versus blood/aspirate-intermediate tobramycin. Viral panel and TB PCR were negative; bronchoscopy was reported without findings.

Worsening AKI and persistent acidosis required continuous renal replacement therapy. He deteriorated despite support within 24 hours; family and palliative discussions led to DNR while mechanical ventilation continued. He subsequently suffered PEA arrest and died within the reported 24-hour interval, with cause of death determined to be S. marcescens cavitary pneumonia complicated by severe septic shock. Current CD4 status and any specific AmpC mechanism are unconfirmed.

ambiguities.issue: Current CD4 not supplied: 181 is last count nine months prior with no unit. Do not import background less-than-70 count, assign current AIDS stage, or assume infection onset source from catheter. Definitive blood culture became available at 48 hours after death; urine/aspirate final result availability times are unstated. Urine tobramycin resistant differs from blood/aspirate intermediate and must not be normalized to a single profile. Discussion suggests AmpC mechanism without assay or gene confirmation. Abstract reports bronchoscopy, but narrative supplies no findings. Clinical death interval within 24 hours retained without invented exact arrest time. Time anchors "within 24 hours of presentation" (deterioration) and "within 24 hours" (death) are not tied to a stated clock time or to each other; the time from arrival to death is not computed. The "48 hours" for the definitive blood culture has no stated anchor (e.g., collection). Authors' statements that HIV-related immunosuppression "likely" compromised pulmonary defenses and that Serratia proteases "may have" contributed to tissue destruction are speculation, not recorded as facts. No MIC values or breakpoints are reported anywhere; susceptibilities are categorical S/I/R only. Discussion of dupilumab-associated Serratia pneumonia (61-year-old man with asthma) concerns a cited published case, not this patient.

evidence.quote: Serratia marcescens is an opportunistic gram-negative bacillus with both intrinsic and acquired resistance mechanisms, making it a challenging pathogen in immunocompromised individuals. We report a fatal case of cavitary pneumonia caused by multidrug-resistant S. marcescens in a 42-year-old HIV-positive man with chronic comorbidities, who presented with acute hypoxic respiratory failure and septic shock. Imaging revealed a large cavitary lesion in the right upper lobe, and cultures from blood, urine, and respiratory secretions confirmed S. marcescens with broad-spectrum antibiotic resistance. Despite aggressive medical management, including broad-spectrum antimicrobials, vasopressor support, bronchoscopy, and renal replacement therapy, the patient’s condition deteriorated, resulting in death. This case underscores the rare but severe pulmonary manifestation of S. marcescens in immunocompromised hosts, emphasizing the importance of early recognition, infection control, and targeted antimicrobial therapy in managing such high-risk infections.

On arrival at the emergency department, he was acutely hypoxic and rapidly deteriorated, requiring urgent intubation. He was found to be in septic shock, with a blood pressure of 72/42 mmHg and a mean arterial pressure of 52 mmHg, necessitating vasopressor support and admission to the intensive care unit (ICU) for close monitoring and management.

Despite aggressive supportive care and broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy, the patient’s clinical condition deteriorated within 24 hours of presentation. Following discussions with the family and the palliative care team, his code status was changed to do-not-resuscitate (DNR), while mechanical ventilation was continued. The patient subsequently suffered a pulseless electrical activity cardiac arrest and expired within 24 hours. The cause of death was determined to be S. marcescens cavitary pneumonia complicated by severe septic shock.

Although cavitary pneumonia due to Serratia is rarely reported [], the formation of pulmonary cavities can result from various pathological processes, including suppurative necrosis (e.g., pyogenic abscess), caseous necrosis (e.g., tuberculosis), ischemic necrosis (e.g., pulmonary infarction), or cystic dilatation of lung structures (e.g., Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia). Malignancy-related cavities may also develop due to internal liquefaction or treatment-induced necrosis. Host factors, such as profound immunosuppression, and pathogen-specific mechanisms influence this tendency []. In HIV patients, Serratia marcescens infection is usually associated with low CD4+ counts of less than 70 cells/ml and an acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) stage (as per CDC, AIDS or stage 3). (2) In our case, advanced immunosuppression due to HIV likely compromised pulmonary defenses, facilitating rapid bacterial proliferation. Furthermore, Serratia’s production of proteases may have contributed to lung tissue destruction, aligning with features of necrotizing pneumonia [].

One of the organism’s notable characteristics is its occasional production of chromosomal AmpC β-lactamase, which can confer resistance to broad-spectrum β-lactam antibiotics and complicate treatment, as observed in our case []. However, S. marcescens is not among the most common AmpC-producing organisms, in contrast to classic HECKY organisms (Enterobacter species, Citrobacter species, and Klebsiella aerogenes). Additionally, S. marcescens possesses other virulence mechanisms, including the production of DNase, lipase, and gelatinase, as well as a pore-forming hemolysin (ShlA) that induces cytotoxicity and promotes inflammatory mediator release [].
